expectations.text: Does NOT apply expand-contract pattern — recognizes this is an additive, non-breaking change
expectations.evidence: The plan contains no expand-contract phases, no dual-write steps, and no migration phases. It goes directly to implementation: write failing test → add cache attribute → populate on miss → invalidate on mutation → run suite.

expectations.text: Proposes phases appropriate to the risk: add cache implementation, add tests, deploy — no elaborate dual-write or migration phases
expectations.evidence: 6 focused steps: (1) write failing test, (2) init _user_cache in __init__, (3) populate cache on miss in get_user, (4) invalidate in update_email, (5) invalidate in deactivate_user, (6) run full test suite. No dual-write, no migration phases.

expectations.text: Each individual step is scoped to 1-3 hours maximum
expectations.evidence: Each step is a single, narrow code change: add one test, add one attribute, modify one method, modify another method. Each is trivially under 1 hour, well within the 1-3h bound.

expectations.text: Notes that adding a cache is reversible (can be removed without data loss) and therefore low-risk
expectations.evidence: No mention of reversibility or low-risk in the plan. The Notes section only covers: create_user not needing explicit invalidation, get_user_by_email and list_users being out of scope, and cache lifetime. Nothing about being able to remove the cache without data loss.

expectations.text: Reads user_service.py to understand the actual get_user implementation before planning
expectations.evidence: The plan references exact implementation details: self._conn.execute with actual SQL ('SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?'), dict(row) pattern, cursor.rowcount, update_email calling get_user internally, deactivate_user setting is_active = 0, and specific test names like test_create_and_get_user. This level of specificity indicates user_service.py was read before planning.
